answers.q3:
LoopLunch should lease the automated washer, but only after it agrees a service response time with the supplier and schedules staff training outside the busiest weeks. The quantitative evidence suggests that the machine improves both efficiency and capacity at current demand.

At present, contribution per subscription is $14, so monthly profit at 3,400 subscriptions is (3,400 × $14) − $42,000 = $5,600. With the washer, contribution rises to $18 while fixed costs become $50,400. At the same demand, monthly profit would therefore be (3,400 × $18) − $50,400 = $10,800. This is an improvement of $5,200 per month. The new break-even output would also be $50,400 ÷ $18 = 2,800 subscriptions, which is 200 below the current break-even output. Capacity would rise from 3,800 to 5,000 subscriptions, giving the business room to grow without immediately adding another washing system.

However, those calculations assume demand and the subscription price stay stable. Higher capacity has little value if LoopLunch cannot attract new customers. The supplier is also young and has limited service staff. A long breakdown could interrupt container availability and collection times. This risk is especially important because the survey shows that dependable collection matters more to customers than new designs. The apparent cost saving could be lost if unreliable operations cause cancellations.

Employee reaction is another concern. Some employees expect less varied work, so imposing automation without consultation could reduce motivation. Retraining them for quality control offers a better approach because it gives staff a continuing role and may improve reliability. Nevertheless, training during the busiest month could temporarily slow operations.

A simple sensitivity check still supports the lease. If demand fell to 3,000 subscriptions, the current system would only break even, while the washer would earn (3,000 × $18) − $50,400 = $3,600. Yet the case gives no installation, training, or cancellation costs, so management should verify those figures before treating the forecast as guaranteed.

Overall, the projected $5,200 monthly profit improvement, lower break-even output, and extra capacity make leasing attractive. I would proceed only if the contract includes maintenance support, management tests the washer before the busiest month, and retraining is planned with employees. These conditions address the strongest qualitative risks while preserving the financial advantage.
